provenance.title: Antenatal danger signs, including the hypertensive-disorders ladder
provenance.primarySource: WHO ANC DAK ANC.DT tables; WHO Managing Complications in Pregnancy and Childbirth; WHO recommendations on antenatal care (2016)
provenance.why: The danger signs that turn a routine antenatal contact into an emergency. The hypertensive disorders are the reason for the schedule's blood-pressure-every-contact rhythm, and they are the family where getting the signal wrong is most lethal.

sourceVerification.vendoredArtefact: docs/reference/who-dak/smart-anc — ANC.DT.01 (danger signs) informs the sign list; the pre-eclampsia thresholds are from WHO guidance, not the DAK decision outputs
sourceVerification.note: ANC.DT.01's own output for a convulsing woman is 'clinician's discretion / proceed with ANC contact OR referral' — a defensible global hedge and an unacceptable national rule, since a convulsing pregnant woman is eclampsia until proven otherwise. This pack does NOT adopt that output; it strengthens it, and says so in ANC_HTN_ECLAMPSIA's adaptation. The sign vocabulary is DAK-derived; the actions are national.

rules.name: Eclampsia — convulsions in pregnancy
rules.message: Eclampsia. Give magnesium sulfate now and control the blood pressure.
rules.explanation: A convulsion in pregnancy is eclampsia until proven otherwise. It is the top of the hypertensive ladder, and the reason the milder hypertensive alerts are suppressed when it fires — three quieter alarms for the same disease would bury this one.
rules.requiredAction: Give magnesium sulfate per protocol, control severe hypertension, protect the airway, and deliver — the definitive treatment is delivery. Do not wait on proteinuria or a second blood pressure.
rules.monitoringInstruction: Magnesium toxicity watch: respiratory rate, reflexes and urine output before and during. Continuous observation.
sourceRefs: WHO Managing Complications in Pregnancy and Childbirth — eclampsia
WHO ANC DAK ANC.DT.01 — danger signs (convulsing)

adaptation.whoStatement: ANC.DT.01 outputs, for a convulsing woman, 'clinician's discretion' and 'proceed with ANC contact OR referral'.
adaptation.nationalStatement: A convulsion in pregnancy is treated as eclampsia: magnesium sulfate and blood-pressure control immediately, delivery as definitive treatment, non-overridable.
adaptation.rationale: The DAK output is a global hedge appropriate to a decision-support tool that must not overstep. As a national rule it is unacceptable — the discretion it defers to is exactly what fails under pressure, and eclampsia untreated for minutes kills. Auto-generating from the DAK row would have shipped the hedge.
evidenceRefs: WHO Managing Complications in Pregnancy and Childbirth — eclampsia
adaptation.applicablePopulation: Any pregnant or recently pregnant woman

rules.name: Pre-eclampsia with severe features
rules.message: Severe pre-eclampsia. Give magnesium sulfate and plan delivery — do not send her home.
rules.explanation: A blood pressure of 160/110 or above, or the severe symptoms — headache, visual disturbance, epigastric pain — mark pre-eclampsia with severe features. Magnesium sulfate prevents the progression to eclampsia. Severe features alone are enough; proteinuria is not required to act.
rules.requiredAction: Give magnesium sulfate, treat severe hypertension, admit, and plan delivery. A severe blood pressure at an outpatient contact is an admission, not a follow-up appointment.
rules.monitoringInstruction: Magnesium toxicity watch. Repeat blood pressure and reassess symptoms.
sourceRefs: WHO Managing Complications in Pregnancy and Childbirth — severe pre-eclampsia
WHO recommendations on antenatal care (2016) — pre-eclampsia prevention and management

adaptation.whoStatement: Blood pressure ≥160/110, or pre-eclampsia with severe symptoms, requires magnesium sulfate and management for severe pre-eclampsia; severe features do not require proteinuria.
evidenceRefs: WHO Managing Complications in Pregnancy and Childbirth — severe pre-eclampsia

testCases.name: BP 165/95 fires on the systolic alone
visual disturbance with a normal BP fires
a normal BP with no severe features does not

rules.name: Pre-eclampsia
rules.message: Pre-eclampsia — new hypertension with proteinuria after 20 weeks.
rules.explanation: Blood pressure 140/90 or above with proteinuria after 20 weeks is pre-eclampsia. It can progress to severe pre-eclampsia and eclampsia, sometimes quickly, so it changes the schedule — more frequent contacts, and a plan for where she will deliver.
rules.requiredAction: Refer for assessment. Increase the frequency of contacts, monitor blood pressure and proteinuria, and counsel her on the danger signs that mean she must come immediately.
rules.monitoringInstruction: Blood pressure and proteinuria at each contact; bloods for platelets, liver and renal function per protocol.
sourceRefs: WHO recommendations on antenatal care (2016) — pre-eclampsia
WHO ANC DAK ANC.DT — blood pressure and proteinuria

adaptation.whoStatement: New-onset hypertension (≥140/90) with proteinuria after 20 weeks of gestation is pre-eclampsia.
evidenceRefs: WHO recommendations on antenatal care (2016) — pre-eclampsia

testCases.name: raised BP with no proteinuria is not pre-eclampsia
before 20 weeks the rule does not apply

rules.name: Gestational hypertension
rules.message: Gestational hypertension — raised blood pressure without proteinuria after 20 weeks.
rules.explanation: New hypertension after 20 weeks without proteinuria. It needs watching because a quarter of these women go on to develop pre-eclampsia, but it is the mildest rung of the ladder — and it is suppressed the moment proteinuria, severe features or a convulsion move her up it.
rules.requiredAction: Monitor more closely: repeat the blood pressure, check proteinuria at every contact, and counsel her on pre-eclampsia danger signs. Refer if it rises or proteinuria appears.
rules.monitoringInstruction: Blood pressure and proteinuria at each contact.
sourceRefs: WHO recommendations on antenatal care (2016) — gestational hypertension

adaptation.whoStatement: New-onset hypertension after 20 weeks without proteinuria is gestational hypertension.
evidenceRefs: WHO recommendations on antenatal care (2016) — gestational hypertension

testCases.name: raised BP without proteinuria after 20 weeks fires
raised BP WITH proteinuria is pre-eclampsia, not this

rules.name: Antepartum haemorrhage
rules.message: Antepartum haemorrhage. Resuscitate and refer — do NOT do a vaginal examination.
rules.explanation: Bleeding after 24 weeks may be placenta praevia or abruption. A digital vaginal examination in praevia can provoke catastrophic haemorrhage, so it is contraindicated until praevia has been excluded by ultrasound.
rules.requiredAction: Resuscitate, get intravenous access and cross-match, and refer urgently to a facility that can perform a caesarean. Do not perform a vaginal examination until placenta praevia is excluded.
rules.monitoringInstruction: Continuous maternal observations and fetal heart. A soft estimate of visible loss underestimates a concealed abruption.
sourceRefs: WHO Managing Complications in Pregnancy and Childbirth — bleeding in later pregnancy

adaptation.whoStatement: Vaginal bleeding after 24 weeks requires resuscitation and urgent referral; vaginal examination is contraindicated until placenta praevia is excluded.
adaptation.nationalStatement: Adopted as published, with the no-vaginal-examination instruction in the required action rather than a footnote.
evidenceRefs: WHO Managing Complications in Pregnancy and Childbirth — bleeding in later pregnancy

rules.name: Reduced fetal movements
rules.message: Reduced fetal movements — assess fetal wellbeing today, not at the next contact.
rules.explanation: A woman's perception that her baby is moving less is associated with stillbirth and must not be reassured away. It is the one thing she notices before anyone measures anything.
rules.requiredAction: Assess the fetal heart and arrange further assessment (cardiotocography or ultrasound) the same day. Do not defer to the next scheduled contact.
rules.monitoringInstruction: If wellbeing cannot be confirmed, refer.
sourceRefs: WHO recommendations on antenatal care (2016) — fetal movement counting

adaptation.whoStatement: WHO does not recommend routine formal fetal-movement counting, citing insufficient evidence of benefit and a risk of harm from intervention.
adaptation.nationalStatement: Routine counting is not mandated, but a woman's spontaneous report of reduced movements triggers same-day assessment.
adaptation.rationale: The WHO position is about routine counting programmes, not about ignoring a woman who says her baby has gone quiet. Those are different things, and conflating them would turn a not-recommended screening programme into a reason to dismiss a presenting symptom associated with stillbirth.
evidenceRefs: WHO recommendations on antenatal care (2016) — fetal movement counting

rules.name: Prelabour rupture of membranes
rules.message: Ruptured membranes before labour — assess for infection and gestation-appropriate management.
rules.explanation: Leaking fluid before labour raises the risk of ascending infection for mother and baby, and the management differs sharply by gestation — a preterm rupture is not a term one.
rules.requiredAction: Confirm rupture, assess for chorioamnionitis (maternal fever, tenderness, offensive liquor, fetal tachycardia), and manage by gestation per protocol. A sterile speculum examination is appropriate; a digital examination increases infection risk and is avoided unless she is in labour.
rules.monitoringInstruction: Temperature and fetal heart; watch for signs of infection.
sourceRefs: WHO Managing Complications in Pregnancy and Childbirth — prelabour rupture of membranes

adaptation.whoStatement: Prelabour rupture of membranes requires assessment for infection and gestation-dependent management.
evidenceRefs: WHO Managing Complications in Pregnancy and Childbirth — prelabour rupture of membranes

rules.name: Fever in pregnancy
rules.message: Fever in pregnancy — find the source; consider malaria, and do not miss sepsis.
rules.explanation: Fever in pregnancy is never just a fever. In this setting malaria must be actively excluded, urinary and genital infection are common, and sepsis is the diagnosis that is missed because the woman compensates until she does not.
rules.requiredAction: Test for malaria, examine for a source (urine, chest, uterus, breast), and assess for sepsis. Treat empirically where sepsis is suspected rather than waiting for a culture.
rules.monitoringInstruction: Repeat observations; a rising pulse with a falling blood pressure is sepsis until proven otherwise.
sourceRefs: WHO recommendations on antenatal care (2016) — infection in pregnancy

adaptation.whoStatement: Fever in pregnancy requires identification and treatment of the source, including malaria where endemic.
evidenceRefs: WHO recommendations on antenatal care (2016) — infection in pregnancy
